turn_text: The president is just absolutely determined to use tariffs with regards to what he hopes will be a better and a more fair trade agreement across the board, whether it be NAFTA or whether it be an individual trade with any country. I think it's a very dangerous road we're taking. Obviously, in terms of retaliation, this is aimed at China. We've already seen what happened with washing machines and solar panels for goodness sakes. The very day that the President was talking about This whole situation was the day that the sorghum producers in Kansas were in my office right next door here. And they had no idea that this was going to come down the pike and that then the Chinese would start an inspection, if you will, to appeal to the WTO. The price of sorghum just, well, the bottom fell out. So they were sitting in my office watching a situation where we had one crop, sorghum, and of course that's in Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, all way up North Dakota, and Arkansas as well. And we saw that price drop precipitously. And it just shows you what that kind of an action can do when number one on the list in terms of retaliation is farm country. Now we've had every commodity group I can imagine in my office sitting in that table over there, and also in the ag-hearing room, 300 from Texas, over 100 from Kansas. We have corn growers, we have wheat growers, especially other soybean growers who really are worried that China will single them out, just at the time when that market for soybeans to China is expanding. So we had Bob Leitheiser in the Finance Committee, and I asked him a lot of questions. about just how much damage he feels in the ag sector that we can stand here in this experiment. Ray Starling of the White House and also Bob Lighthizer said, look, we understand that agriculture could be singled out. And if so, there ought to be a way of doing something on an executive basis with the Secretary of Agriculture to ameliorate that. What that is, I'm not quite sure. So here we are trying to ride a farm bill. We have this big dust up with tariffs. It's just most unfortunate. I don't think that this is the way we should be going. We have yet to see any kind of a major grain sale, or for that matter, any kind of effort on a trade deal, whether it be the former members of the TPP or anybody else should be trading. We had Taiwan sitting right there where you're sitting, saying that this would really harm their sovereignty with regards to what China does to them and if we in turn put sanctions or a tariff on Taiwan. And that goes for a lot of different countries that have been our allies. So that's a question. I think we're going at this in a way that really represents a danger to agriculture. And the irony of it is we are experiencing economic growth minus the stock market here in the last couple days. But I think that will come back. And we could do so much damage in farm country that it could really eat at whatever economic recovery we're having. That'd be a paradox of enormous irony that we pass a tax bill. We see economic recovery and then we have a trade policy that works in a very counterproductive way.
